cards.front: What is an ecosystem?
back: A community of organisms interacting with each other and the non-living environment.

cards.front: Give one biotic component of an ecosystem.
back: Plants.

cards.front: Name the process by which plants release water vapour.
back: Transpiration.

cards.front: What is coral bleaching?
back: Coral turning white after expelling its symbiotic algae.

cards.front: Name the rainforest case study used in this course.
back: The Peruvian Amazon.

cards.front: Name the coral reef case study used in this course.
back: Andros Barrier Reef, The Bahamas.

cards.front: Explain why tropical rainforests have rapid nutrient cycling.
back: Heat and moisture cause dead material to decompose quickly.
Dense roots rapidly absorb the released nutrients.

cards.front: Give two ways in which coral reefs are valuable to people.
back: They support fishing and tourism income.
They absorb wave energy and protect coasts.

cards.front: Explain why rainforest soils may lose fertility after trees are cleared.
back: The nutrient store in vegetation is removed.
Heavy rain then leaches nutrients from exposed soil.

cards.front: Give two threats to the Peruvian Amazon.
back: Farming or cattle ranching.
Mining, road building or logging.

cards.front: Explain why warm-water coral reefs are found in shallow, clear seas.
back: The algae living in coral need sunlight for photosynthesis.
Clear, shallow water allows enough light to reach them.

cards.front: Give two local strategies used to protect Andros Barrier Reef.
back: Marine protected areas.
Sustainable fishing, monitoring or eco-tourism.

cards.front: Explain one example of interdependence in a tropical rainforest.
back: Trees provide food and habitats for animals.
Animals may pollinate flowers or spread seeds.
This helps trees reproduce, so each group supports the other.

cards.front: Explain how deforestation can change the rainforest water cycle.
back: Fewer leaves intercept rainfall.
Less water returns to the atmosphere through transpiration.
Surface runoff rises and local rainfall recycling may fall.

cards.front: Explain how climate controls the distribution of hot deserts.
back: Many occur around 20–30° north and south.
Descending air creates high pressure and prevents cloud formation.
Rainfall is therefore very low, producing sparse vegetation.

cards.front: Explain how a marine protected area may improve reef health.
back: Damaging fishing or development is restricted.
Fish populations and habitats have time to recover.
A healthier food web can make the reef more resilient.

cards.front: Explain two adaptations of tropical rainforest plants.
back: **Drip-tip leaves** shed heavy rain quickly, reducing water damage and fungal growth.
**Buttress roots** spread near the surface and support tall trees where soil is shallow and nutrient-poor.

cards.front: Explain two ways the Peruvian Amazon is valuable.
back: It stores carbon and recycles water, helping regulate climate and rainfall.
It supplies habitats, food, materials and livelihoods for Indigenous communities and businesses.

cards.front: Explain two threats to Andros Barrier Reef.
back: High sea temperatures cause bleaching because coral expels its algae and loses a major food source.
Pollution or sediment reduces water quality and blocks sunlight needed by the algae.

cards.front: Explain why clearing rainforest may create short-term gains but long-term costs.
back: Farming, mining and timber can create jobs, exports and tax income.
However, habitat and stored carbon are lost, soils erode and water cycling is disrupted, weakening future livelihoods.
